1.q: The Hirshhorn Museum installed a wallpaper by this artist featuring gold security cameras, titled The Animal That Looks Like A Llama But Is Really An Alpaca. 1.q: After producing his Peacocks and Peonies in this medium,John La Farge became mired in a patent dispute with another artist. 1.q: Otto Nicolai founded this city's premier orchestra, which uses a type of horn with double-cylinder pushrod valves and a more mellow sound than the double horn. The harpist Anna Lelkes became the first permanent female member of that orchestra in 1997. The Warriors, a Marsden Hartley painting, was used as a backdrop for this work when it was photographed for the journal The Blind Man by Alfred Stieglitz. Wildlife-inspired fashion by a designer from this country include dresses made of ostrich feathers and clamshells, as well as his final show Plato's Atlantis. That designer ended a 2006 show by projecting an illusion of a model from this country dancing in a white chiffon wedding dress. A tartan-inclined designer from this country ran the punk boutique SEX ("sex") and often drew from its (*) Teddy Boy subculture. 1.q: One character in this musical sings for his "dark-eyed beauty" to "have another drink" as he has "one more night left here in town." For 10 points, name this plucked Hindustani instrument played by Vilayat Khan and Ravi Shankar.

A sculptor from this country created four slabs of rock with round holes in them for her large Four Square (Walk Through) sculpture. A couple hold onto an infant in a World War II memorial designed by an artist from this country called The Family Group. Another sculptor from this country was inspired by Chac-Mools to create various Reclining Figures. For 10 points, name this country home to Damien Hirst and Henry Moore.

A dolphin-riding cupid clings to the right leg of a sculpture of one of these people, whose cuirass depicts the return of a stolen battle standard. A pair of cornucopias surrounds a shield at the base of a statue of one of these men. An upward-pointing hand and a head with enormous eyes remain as fragments of a colossal statue of one of these people. One of these men carries a club and wears the jaws and pelt of the (*) Nemean lion in a bust depicting him as Hercules. 1.r: Roman emperors [or word forms; or Caesar; or Augustus; or imperator; or princeps; prompt on soldier or warrior or equivalents]

1.q: This modern-day country titles a highly geometric rendition of a Lancaster grain elevator by Charles Demuth. Edmonia Lewis depicted an ancient leader of this country dead on a throne. Some of the best surviving examples of Roman painting are funerary portraits on wooden boards in this country. 1.r: Egypt [or Arab Republic of Egypt; accept Ancient Egypt; accept My Egypt; accept the Flight from Egypt]

1.q: This material was used for several pieces produced in Longquan during the Song Dynasty. Pieces made from it were often decorated using cords of rope. This material was used for "Am I Not a Man And a Brother?" It's mostly made of kaolinite, and types of it include celadon. Asian pieces in this material were imitated by craftsmen in Delft. A kind of it that integrates bone powder was made by Josiah (*) Wedgewood, and it comes in soft- and hard-paste kinds. It's often decorated in blue and white. Qin Shi Huang Di's tomb contains an "army" made of this material, which vitrifies, or turns glassy, at high temperatures. For 10 points, name this material, types of which include terracotta and porcelain.
1.r: ceramics [accept any answer to do with pottery, or any more specific type of ceramic, e.g. earthenware, terracotta, porcelain, china, etc.]

1.q: Claude Brown described growing up in this city in his autobiographical novel Manchild in the Promised Land, and this city provides the setting for the works in Joseph Mitchell's Up In The Old Hotel. William Shawn was the longtime editor of a publication in this city, and Jane Jacobs opposed an urban planner working in this city who was profiled by Robert (*) Caro in his book The Power Broker; that planner was Robert Moses. Kaolinite was used by Chinese artists to produce iconic (*) blue-and-white forms of this artwork that was exported throughout the Islamic world. Calyxes and Kraters were decorated by red and black-figure painting as part of this art form, which involves shaping and firing dried greenware until it becomes durable. For 10 points, name this art form that transforms ceramics into usable objects.
1.r: pottery [anti-prompt on earthenware, porcelain, terra cotta, and other specific forms]

1.q: Description acceptable. A heckler's call for a dentist during this event was reportedly sparked by the sight of "knock-kneed and long-braided Lolitas jumping up and down." 1.q: Athena Tacha traced the development of a common subject throughout this artist's career; the most famous depiction of that subject caused controversy when Edward Steichen purchased and shipped it. This artist of Mademoiselle Pogany used bronze and marble to sculpt a woman's head (*) leaning to the right. 1.q: Kaia Gerber recreated a black floral Dior type of these items worn by Bianca Jagger that is often misattributed to Halston, though Halston did design Bianca Jagger's red sequined one of these items. In October 1926, Vogue published a sketch of one of these items that it compared to the Ford Model T. A 1974 Bob Mackie design for Cher ["share"] and an item worn by Marilyn Monroe to sing "Happy Birthday" are (*) "naked" examples of this garment. Mrinalni Mukherjee ("m-ree-NAL-nee MOOK-er-jee") has made many statues of deities using this material. El Anatsui produces his own form of this material using bottle caps, following the kente method. David Bowie's song "Joe the Lion" references a work of this type involving a Volkswagen Beetle titled Trans-Fixed. 1.r: performance art [prompt on crucifixion after “Joe the Lion” with “What general type of art was the crucifixion a part of?”; do not accept or prompt on “performing arts”]

1.q: One of these objects represents Sojourner Truth with three faces inspired by African masks sharing a single body. Over 1000 of these objects were painted with blue paint in an art exhibit about capital punishment by Julie L. Green. Thirty-nine of these objects painted with motifs that resemble a vulva or a butterfly form part of an installation artwork at the Brooklyn Museum that also includes the names of (*) 999 women on tiles surrounding them. After John the Baptist was killed on the orders of Salome, his head was often depicted as placed on one of these objects. Pei designed the interior of a Midtown Manhattan hotel named after these things. After two characters discover they are (*) HIV-positive, the cast of Rent sings a song titled "[these things] of Love." For 10 points, name these phenomena, four of which title a concerto by Vivaldi.
1.r: seasons [accept The Seasons, Frankie Vallie and the Four Seasons, The Four Seasons Hotel, Seasons of Love, The Four Seasons]

1.q: The creator of the mini-crini ran this city's boutique shop SEX and was influential in this city's 1970s punk scene. Astor Piazzolla is a composer from, for 10 points, what nation, the home of tango?

2.q: Containers attached to these items can be opened by moving a bead on a cord supported by a type of round miniature sculpture commonly made of ivory or boxwood. 2.q: After leaving the band Ash Ra Tempel, an artist from this country recorded the hour-long, chess-inspired track E2-E4. 2.r: Germany [or West Germany; or Federal Republic of Germany; or Deutschland]

2.q: As mayor of Bogota, Antanas Mockus hired 420 members of this profession to mock people into adhering to traffic laws. 2.q: A predecessor to one type of this instrument popular in the 1920's was called the snowshoe. Indian religious ceremonies use a variant of this Western instrument called a manjira or taal. 2.r: cymbals [or hi-hat cymbals; or crash cymbals; or ride cymbals; prompt on “percussion” or “drums” or “drum set” with “what specific percussion instrument?”]

2.q: On the last day of The Artist is Present, seven guards escorted Josephine Decker away after she performed this action. 2.q: A current resident of this metropolis published an early artist book titled Twentysix Gasoline Stations and collected photographs of thoroughfares in this city taken with a motorized camera. 2.q: This state is the setting of Jeremy Karoff's 2014 short documentary Cavedigger, which profiles Ra Paulette, who excavates elaborate sandstone caves in this state. Painter Bert Geer Phillips founded an "art (*) colony" in this state that was frequently the home of art patron Mabel Dodge Luhan and author D.H. Lawrence. While living at Ghost Ranch in this state, the wife of Alfred Stieglitz painted many animal skulls and desert scenes. 2.q: This system adopted Sprague-Thomson stock in the wake of a disastrous 1903 fire. Two inaccessible and never-used parts of this system are called Haxo and Porte Molitor. This system connects in several places with the RER and the SNCF. After the death of Abdelbaki Sahraoui, the GIA carried out a series of attacks on this system in 1995. Tiles spelling out the text of the (*) Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen decorate a part of this system that inspired Ezra Pound to write a poem describing the "apparition of these faces in the crowd". This system features a number of Art Nouveau-styled cast iron entrances designed by Hector Guimard. Its 303 stations include two serving Orly and Charles de Gaulle airports. For 10 points, name this French public transit system.
2.r: the Paris Métro [prompt on partial answers; accept Paris Métropolitain or Métro de Paris; prompt on “Métro” or “the Paris subway” or equivalents]

2.q: This modern-day country was home to the periodical Everyman His Own Football, which is often considered the first zine. A leader of this country is X-rayed to show gold coins in his stomach in a work by John (*) Heartfield. 2.q: A member of this movement helped organize its "first international fair" after changing his name, in a protest against anti-British sentiment, to John Heartfield. 2.q: A fashion designer with this first name dressed the drag queen Marcia Pantera and designed skull prints that gained popularity among his country's youth rebel culture; that designer's surname is Herchcovitch. Diet Prada aired Owen Mooney's sexual assault allegations against another designer with this first name who succeeded Nicolas Ghesquiere ["ghess-kiare"] at Balenciaga. A hologram of (*) Kate Moss used in a runway show by a designer with this first name was revived for the exhibition "Savage Beauty." Sarah Burton presented the unfinished collection "Angels and Demons" after a designer with this first name committed suicide in 2010. For 10 points, give this first name shared by Chinese American designer Wang and British designer McQueen.
2.r: Alexander [or Alexandre; or Alexandre Herchcovitch; or Alexander Wang; or Alexander McQueen]

2.q: In 2007, 15 visitors to a museum in this country were injured by a large crack in a floor that constituted Doris Salcedo's installation Shibboleth. A curator from this country named Nicholas Serota makes an "Acquisitions Decision" while looking at red underwear in a painting from a movement founded in this country, Stuckism. An art museum in this country exhibited installations like Olafur Eliasson's The Weather Project and Ai Weiwei's (*) Sunflower Seeds in its Turbine Hall. For 10 points, name this country home to the YBA, which frequently exhibits their work at the Tate Modern in London.
2.r: United Kingdom [ or Great Britain; accept England]

2.q: One of these objects names a Jacqulyn Buglisi piece in which 150 whiteclad dancers memorialized 9/11 victims at the Lincoln Center. It's not a chair, but Marcel Breuer used tubular steel instead of wood to vary upon Josef Albers' colorful design for a "nesting" set of these objects at the Bauhaus. Herman Miller popularized one of these objects with a base of two curved rosewood boards designed by Isamu (*) Noguchi. The Endless Column and Gate of the Kiss can be found alongside one of these objects surrounded by twelve hourglasses at Targu Jiu. Constantin Brancusi made one of these objects "of Silence." For 10 points, name these objects on which Judy Chicago's Dinner Party is served.
2.r: tables [or the Noguchi Table; or Table of Silence]

2.q: Along with the drums, this is the most common instrument used in modern performances of an elaborate English folk dance in which participants wear bells and toss sticks back and forth, the Morris dance. With a rhythm section made of a triangle and a zabumba, the Brazilian forro dance is performed to music played by this instrument. Bands playing the "Slovenian style" or "Cleveland style" of a (*) Central European dance always feature one of these instruments. Astor Piazzolla's nuevo tango style heavily featured the bandoneon, a relative of this instrument. Weird Al Yankovic plays this instrument, which is heavily used in polka music. For 10 points, name this instrument that is played by pressing buttons or keys and expanding or contracting the bellows.
2.r: accordion [accept melodeon, concertina, or bandonéon before mention]

2.q: A 1944 exhibition titled The Imagery of [this activity] featured objects used for this activity created by Max Ernst. This activity is depicted in another work with violin scroll, flask, and pyramid-shaped objects made from brass, silver and gold. In the Rene Clair film Entr'acte, Man Ray engages in this activity with another artist who spent the later part of his career engaging in this activity after the creation of a work subtitled (*) The Large Glass. A group of objects used for this activity include one discovered in Ager, Catalonia, as well as one discovered in the Hebrides on the island of Lewis made from walrus ivory. Marcel Duchamp became a master in, for 10 points, what game, which was depicted by Man Ray in the queen's gambit declined position?
2.r: chess [or phrases like “playing chess”]

2.q: The music of this country often makes use of the chord progression (read slowly) "four major 7, five 7, three minor 7, 6 minor," which is nicknamed the "royal road" progression. This country's enka music is a form of sentimental ballad music and has similarities with blues. A loosely defined, broad genre of this country's music that arose in the 1970s and 80s is labeled "city pop." A music (*) software developed in this country uses a 16-year-old girl with long, turquoise twintails as its mascot. Virtual idols using the Vocaloid software are popular in this country. For 10 points, name this home country of Hatsune Miku, where J-pop is often used for anime openings.
2.r: Japan

2.q: The colotomic structure of this musical style marks off nested cycles by using interpunctuating instruments. This musical style uses notably stretched "pseudo-octaves" since its main melodic instruments are highly inharmonic. In this style, instruments are often played in pairs tuned apart to cause interference beating and a "shimmering" timbre. Bourgault-Ducoudray's ["boor-GO du-ku-DRAY"] rhapsody imitating this style was performed at the (*) 1889 Exposition Universelle, where it inspired Claude Debussy. Wayang shadow puppet plays are accompanied by music in this style, which uses instruments like the kenong and saron and is built on the slendro and pelog scales. For 10 points, name this musical style whose ensembles center on pitched metal percussion, the primary traditional music of Indonesia.
2.r: gamelan [or gambelan; before "Indonesia", prompt on Indonesian music]

2.q: In 2002, an artist from this non-US country wore a suit made of meat to protest the War on Terror as part of the performance piece My New York. That artist from this country shed light on this country's poor sanitation by sitting on a public toilet covered in honey. Another artist born in this country created the memorial video 4851 and made a sculpture of a hand giving the middle finger as a part of his (*) Study of Perspective. In 2011, the Tate Museum hung a sign requesting the release from prison of that artist from this country who also created the exhibit Sunflower Seeds. That artist from this country helped design a steel stadium known as the Bird's Nest for the 2008 Summer Olympics. For 10 points, name this home country of Ai Weiwei ["eye way-way"].
2.r: The People’s Republic of China [or PRC or Zhōngguó or Zhōnghuá Rénmín Gònghéguó]

2.q: Many of the best-preserved historical examples of these objects come from Transylvania, where they were used to decorate Lutheran churches. One style of these objects depicts one or more hanging lamps above a keyhole and is named for their frequent depiction by Bellini. These objects often depict a pair of columns on opposite sides of their central arched feature. Less-common rotationally-symmetric forms of these objects depict a mirrored double niche, though they more typically depict a single niche representing a (*) mihrab. When in use, these objects are oriented to face the qibla, and large numbers of them cover the floors of mosques. For 10 points, name these woven objects on which Muslims prostrate during salah.
2.r: prayer rugs [or prayer mats; or sajjāda; or seccade; or namazlık; or jānamāz; prompt on rugs, carpets, or mats]

2.q: Theodore Dalrymple wrote an article in City Journal that analyzed Le Corbusier's artwork and how it equated him to this phenomenon, placing emphasis on the idea that he and his disciples claimed to create universal "states of mind" in artwork that others could not comprehend. Slavoj Zizek divided this phenomenon into four facets, one of which was the idea that it arose out of an existential closure of thought. A book titled for this concept claims "intellectual, spiritual, and artistic initiative" to be as dangerous to (*) it as mob rule, and is notably divided into three essays including "Antisemitism" and "Imperialism". Hannah Arendt discussed this concept and its ideological appeal by comparing Nazism and Stalinism. For 10 points, name this political concept, characterized by absolute power in the state controlling both public and private life.
2.r: totalitarianism [prompt on “authoritarianism” or “dictatorship”]

2.q: One character in this work is laughed at after announcing that his wife cheated on him with Fred Motz. A bottle of a perfume called Nostalgia is broken in anger after one character learns her father's identity, which causes the collapse of a castle in this work. One character in this work writes "Good joke. Everybody laugh" about a joke he heard with the punchline (*) "I am Pagliacci." One character in this work decides life has meaning and calls it a "thermodynamic miracle" after fleeing to Mars to escape accusations that he is responsible for the cancer of characters including Janey Slater. Another character in this work cuts up a dress he made for Kitty Genovese to create a mask and has the real name Walter Kovacs. Rorschach discovers Ozymandias' plan for a false flag alien attack on New York in, for 10 points, what graphic novel by Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons?
2.r: Watchmen
2.c: 2020 DECAMERON Pkt Marcelo Agachate y Concelo Q27

2.q: One of these objects titles a 1972 performance art piece held in Los Angeles' Market Street gallery in which Chris Burden refused to speak for twenty-two days. In 1991, a series of monochrome billboards depicting one of these objects were put up throughout New York City by Felix Gonzalez-Torres. A sign reading "Hair Peace" was displayed in a series of protests during the honeymoon of John Lennon and Yoko Ono named for these objects and their similarity to (*) sit-ins. In another artwork, empty vodka bottles and blood-stained underwear are placed near a disheveled one of these objects belonging to Tracey Emin. A Black maid attends to a nude woman reclining on one of these objects in Edouard Manet's Olympia. For 10 points, name this piece of furniture which Vincent van Gogh depicted in his room In Arles.
2.r: beds [accept mattresses; accept Bedroom In Arles; accept My Bed; accept bed-ins; accept Bed-Ins for Peace; accept Bed Piece]

2.q: Beethoven's Triple Concerto is most often played by a glamorous all-female trio from Juilliard ("JOO-lee-ard") named for this word. The trio section of a solo piano piece titled for this adjective begins with 6 rolled E major chords before a fast left-hand ostinato of E, D-sharp, C-sharp, and B octaves. That Opus 53 solo piece titled for this adjective begins with a loud E-flat octave in both hands, then chromatic ascending first-inversion triads. This adjective sometimes names a composer's middle period spanning the decade after (*) 1803. George Sand gave this nickname to a Polonaise in A-flat major after the 1848 Revolution in France. Before a funeral march in C minor, two E-flat major tutti chords open a symphony titled for this adjective originally dedicated to Napoleon. For 10 points, what adjective names a Chopin polonaise and Beethoven's triumphant Third Symphony?
2.r: heroic [accept Eroica Symphony; accept Heroic Polonaise or Polonaise héroïque; accept Eroica Trio; accept heroic period or heroic phase or heroic style; prompt on polonaise or Polish by asking “what’s the other title word?”]

2.q: Carlton Barrett popularized a form of this musical concept called "one drop." Forms of this concept that have been the "now" thing include Sleng Teng, Diwali, and Real Rock. A common form of this concept for the "underground style" was inspired by Shabba Ranks after it was embraced by immigrants to Panama. The Jamaican Patois word for this concept names instrumentals frequently used in many different times and sung over by a deejay in (*) dancehall. A ubiquitous form of this element in reggaeton is called dembow. In calypso, this musical element is often defined by an instrument first made with industrial cargo containers. Modern reggae music often uses the "four on the floor" style of this element, which is also used in disco. For 10 points, name this element of Caribbean music often maintained with steelpans and drums.
2.r: rhythm [or the beat; accept riddim]

2.q: A young Claude Debussy was "crushed" by living in this city after writing a cantata, though he completed the vibrant suite Printemps ("pran-TOM") in this city. Berlioz left this city to kill his ex, and wrote the cantata Herminie ("air-mee-NEE") in one of four attempts to live in this city. Half the cellos tune their lowest string down to B to play faint marching tritones before a slithery English horn solo right after a nocturne set in this city fades out a phonograph recording of a chirping (*) nightingale. In 1913, Lili Boulanger ("boo-lawn-ZHAY") was the first woman to win a prestigious French scholarship named for this city. A tone poem trilogy set in this city depicts four "festivals," and certain objects in the Janiculum ("juh-NICK-yoo-lum"), a catacomb, and the Villa Borghese ("bor-GAY-zay"). Ottorino Respighi ("res-PEE-ghee") depicted the "Pines" of, for 10 points, what city's Appian Way?
2.r: Rome [or Roma; accept Prix de Rome, Pines of Rome, Pini di Roma, Roman Festivals, or Feste Romane]

2.q: Satin flats first sold by a fashion brand from this country helped popularize the "balletcore" aesthetic in the mid-2010s. It's not Georgia nor Russia, but a line of silk "pyjamas" glamorous enough to wear at galas was debuted by a designer who mainly resided in this country named Irene Galitzine. Before creating the "shoe hat," a designer born in this country gifted Wallis Simpson a dinner dress featuring a hand painting of a lobster. This country is home to (*) Miu Miu, a subsidiary of a fashion house from this country known for leather and Re-Nylon handbags. "Shocking pink" is the signature color of a surrealist designer from this country who had a fierce rivalry with Coco Chanel. For 10 points, name this birth country of fashion designers Elsa Schiaparelli ("SKYAHP-a-rel-ee") and Miuccia Prada.
2.r: Italy [or Italian Republic or Italia or Repubblica Italiana]

2.q: In one of this piece's slow movements, harp-like flutes oscillate B and A half-diminished chords in a plodding ostinato that builds up to a climax with tubular bells. This piece's fourth movement begins with layers of rising, shimmering violins cycling groups of three 16th notes like "E, G, A" before the horns introduce four bouncy themes in triple meter before a majestic "hymn" trio section. Low strings and timpani maintain a steadily (*) crescendoing G ostinato in a "short-short-short long, long, short-short long" pattern to open this piece's first movement, which shares its 5/4 ("five-four") time signature with its final movement, which ends with a choral fadeout and is subtitled "The Mystic." A section about "The Bringer of Jollity" appears in, for 10 points, what Gustav Holst suite that opens with "Mars, The Bringer of War"?
2.r: The Planets

2.q: Description acceptable. A massive sculpture of an artwork in this medium is located in Vegreville, Alberta and only received funding because it was dedicated to the centennial of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The "Star Rosette" is one of the most popular designs in this medium. Veesk and kistkas are used to make artworks in this medium, which often include symbols like "eternity bands" and berehynia motifs. Artworks in this medium are made by drawing (*) wax patterns using a stylus on a certain object and then placing that object in a series of dyes in the wax-resist method. A term for this medium comes from the Ukrainian verb for "to write". For 10 points, name this medium in which colorful patterns representing Christ's resurrection are painted onto an edible substance that you might hard-boil.
2.r: Ukrainian Easter eggs [or pysanka; or pysanky; prompt on eggs or painted eggs or dyed eggs by asking “for which occasion?”]

2.q: In Neo Yokio, Kaz Kaan battles a work by this artist possessed by a demon. This artist created The Fate of a Banished Man for an exhibit that he claimed was collected by a freed slave named Cif Amotan II. That exhibit by this artist has a namesake pseudo-documentary about its works being recovered from the bottom of the ocean, titled Treasures from the Wreck of the Unbelievable. This artist of In and Out of Love is controversial for his mass slaughter of (*) butterflies for a number of works. This artist placed a bug zapper, a colony of flies, and a cow head together in a box for his work A Thousand Years, and he bejeweled a skull to create For the Love of God. For 10 points, which Young British Artist's The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living consists of a tiger shark suspended in formaldehyde?
2.r: Damien Steven Hirst

2.q: A short piece in this genre by Dmitri Shostakovich parodies a march in 7/8 ("seven-eight") time and Hanon exercises in its final themes and was written for his son's 19th birthday. Apocryphally, a blind Ukrainian beggar's tune provided the first theme of another Russian piece in this genre that opens with the unrecapitulated motif [read slowly] "F, D-flat, C, B-flat" played by loud horns. Vladimir Horowitz popularized a challenging D minor piece in this genre written the same year as the composer's tone poem The (*) Isle of the Dead. Low F's alternate with eight crescendoing block chords, often described as "bell-like," to open the second piece in this genre by Sergei Rachmaninoff. For 10 points, name this genre of 27 Mozart pieces and Beethoven's "Emperor" in which an orchestra accompanies a keyboard soloist.
2.r: piano concerto [or piano concerti; prompt on concerto] (The second sentence describes Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1.)

2.q: Auguste Tolbecque ("oh-GOOST tol-BECK") premiered a single-movement A minor concerto for this instrument, the first one by Camille Saint-Saens ("kuh-MEE san-SAWNS"). Pierre Fournier ("foorn-YAY"), Maurice Marechal ("mah-ray-SHAHL"), Paul Tortelier, and Auguste Franchomme ("frawn-SHUM") played this instrument. This instrument and piano play in the C minor Elegie ("ay-lay-ZHEE") by Gabriel Faure ("for-AY"). A piece often played as a solo for this instrument was chosen by Michel Fokine ("foh-KEEN") as music for a short dance choreographed for (*) Anna Pavlova ("AH-nah puhv-LOH-vah"). That solo piece for this instrument is the penultimate movement of Carnival of the Animals and is titled "Le Cygne" ("luh seen"), or "The Swan." Pablo Casals ("kuh-ZALLS") made his name by recording J. S. Bach's six solo suites for this instrument. For 10 points, name this large string instrument held between the knees and played by Yo-Yo Ma.
2.r: cello (The Fokine choreography is The Dying Swan.)

2.q: This composer embraced Christian Science in New York, where he ran into clarinetist Simeon Bellison, whose klezmer band Zimro ("ZIM-raw") just toured the Far East and contained a string quartet and piano; Bellison sent this composer a notebook of Hebrew themes that he quickly worked into an Overture for them. Before finishing a ballet with four seasonal fairies, he extracted three piano pieces from it, including a plucky, chromatic gavotte. His Symphony No. 1 in D major, scored entirely in concert pitch, imitates (*) Haydn's style and also includes a brief gavotte with "wrong notes." Galina Ulanova premiered the title roles of his Cinderella and a ballet whose three suites include "Dance of the Knights" and "Death of Tybalt." For 10 points, what composer of the "Classical Symphony" returned from exile to Soviet Russia and wrote Romeo and Juliet and Peter and the Wolf?
2.r: Sergei Prokofiev (The first clue is about Overture on Hebrew Themes.)

2.q: In 2018, Cori Bostic became the first woman to lead one of these groups founded by P. A. Van Weller. These groups still follow a "Guide" written by William P. Foster, who modernized how these groups operated during his tenure as director of "The 100." In 2023, an exhibition featuring these groups called "The Honda" was relocated from Atlanta to Montgomery. These groups "throw punches" to win "battles" that often occur in informal time periods called the (*) "Zero Quarter" and "Fifth Quarter." They're not sports teams, but these groups name a rivalry game between Jackson State University and Southern University called the BoomBox Classic. These groups are often accompanied by baton twirlers and flag spinners. For 10 points, name these ensembles led by a drum major.
2.r: HBCU marching bands [or HBCU bands; accept historically black colleges and universities in place of HBCUs; prompt on bands]

2.q: Claw-shaped examples of these objects named for armadillos featured in Alexander McQueen's Plato's Atlantis collection. Meret Oppenheim placed these objects upside-down on a plate and trussed like a turkey in My Nurse. Vivienne Westwood created blue, crocodile-patterned examples of these objects infamously modeled by Naomi Campbell. A black hat resembling one of these objects was designed by Elsa (*) Schiaparelli. The vertically interlocking letters "YSL" offer structural support in another line of these objects. The blue Hangisi examples of these objects are designed by Manolo Blahnik with needle-thin points. Designs for the Pigalle ("pee-GAHL") and So Kate originated in their creator's use of nail polish to cover black bottoms on these objects. For 10 points, Christian Louboutin placed iconic red soles on stilettos, an example of what kind of shoe?
2.r: high heels [accept stilettos until read; accept pumps; prompt on shoes or boots]

2.q: This artist copied Horst P. Horst's photograph of a woman's back and a Mainbocher Corset for a scene in one of her music videos. The Catholic Church boycotted Pepsi for using one of this artist's songs in commercials. That song by this artist juxtaposes images of the KKK burning crosses with the stigmata. During her "Blonde Ambition" tour, this artist controversially sported Jean-Paul (*) Gaultier's cone bra. This artist popularized "Don't Cry for Me Argentina" after starring in a movie adaptation of Evita. David Fincher directed the black-and-white music video for this artist's most famous song, in which she rhymes the phrase "strike a pose" with the title word. For 10 points, name this American pop singer of "Like a Virgin" and "Vogue."
2.r: Madonna [or Louise Ciccone]

2.q: To please this person, a statue of a triton copied from a Gian Lorenzo Bernini fountain was made with its mouth curving upward so that it would "smile." In a structure named for this person, Manuel Rosales helped construct an organ nicknamed "Hurricane Mama" that resembles French fries. Michael Graves designed a pair of sister hotels named for this person that feature statues of a (*) swan and a dolphin respectively. A "magic wand" was added to a sphere featured at an "experimental prototype community of tomorrow" envisioned by this man. Curved stainless steel panels compose a structure named for this person that houses performances of the Los Angeles Philharmonic. For 10 points, identify this namesake of a Frank Gehry-designed concert hall and a Florida theme park called his "world."
2.r: Walt Disney [prompt on Disney; accept Walt Disney Concert Hall or Walt Disney World Swan or Walt Disney World Dolphin] (The “community of tomorrow” was realized as the Epcot theme park.)

2.q: In 2002, Vivienne Westwood debuted a "VW" design based on this symbol that she later allowed for commercial use in a collaboration with the Rug Company. After calling one Gucci dress "boring," its wearer asked her sister Natalie to add a peace sign and this symbol to the ensemble. During a 2021 performance, Dua Lipa wore a jacket whose design was inspired by a dress with a towel containing this symbol stitched onto it. This symbol is emblazoned on the logo window of Classics shoes sold by (*) Reebok. Geri Halliwell stoked patriotic sentiments by wearing a minidress emblazoned with this symbol during a 1997 Spice Girls performance. For 10 points, promoters of the Cool Britannia movement often integrated what flag design into their fashion?
2.r: Union Jack [or Union Flag; accept flag of the United Kingdom or flag of the UK; accept flag of Great Britain; accept British flag; prompt on flags]

2.q: In 2017, this fashion label debuted an "anti-perfume" fragrance marketed as smelling like concrete. This fashion label's 1995 "Sleep" collection of striped outfits was lambasted for resembling slacks worn at Auschwitz. Dresses representing nine different themes of dualism were prepared by this fashion label's founder for the 2017 "Art of the In-Between" Met Gala. Filip Pagowski designed the (*) logo for this fashion label's PLAY collection. Collaborations with this fashion label, including an iconic one with Converse, typically feature the emblazoning of red heart emblems with eyes throughout the garment. This Japanese fashion label was founded by Rei Kawakubo. For 10 points, name this fashion label whose name is French for "like boys."
2.r: Comme des Garçons [or CDG]

2.q: In this work, one of the lead characters has dream where he is haunted by spirits of Johnnie Cochran, Genghis Khan, Adolf Hitler, and dancing cups of coffee as the devil plays the guitar. Another character constantly complains about having maggots in his scrotum. Its two lead characters join the natives in the singing of "Hasa Diga Eebowai" after having their bags stolen by the soldiers of (*) General-Butt-Fucking-Naked but soon stop once they realize that they're singing "Fuck you God." As it opens, Elder Cunningham is accused of "making things up again" after he says "Would you like to change religions? I have a book written by Jesus!" For 10 points, name this Matt Stone and Trey Parker musical about a religion founded by Joseph Smith.
2.r: The Book of Mormon

2.q: Jason and Matt compete for the role of a character from this literary work in a coming-of-age rock musical by Damon Intrabartolo titled Bare. May and Angelique come to the rescue of a character adapted from this literary work in a musical in which Lance harshly orders his son Francois around. A 2019 Max Martin musical that reworks this work's ending includes the tune "Problem/Can't Feel My Face." In a musical inspired by this work, a character represented by the leitmotif C - F sharp - G pities (*) "any girl who isn't me tonight" and is "loved by a pretty wonderful boy." This play inspired a musical with choreography by Jerome Robbins in which "Somewhere" is sung by Tony and Maria, the latter of whom sings "I Feel Pretty." The Sharks and the Jets from West Side Story were inspired by, for 10 points, what Shakespeare play's Montagues and Capulets?
2.r: Romeo and Juliet [or The Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet]

2.q: A major scholar of this era and director of the Courtauld Institute for thirty years was revealed to be an ex-Soviet spy by Margaret Thatcher. The study of patronage in painting was kick-started by a book about this era by Francis Haskell. This era, which was studied by Anthony Blunt, was largely rehabilitated by Heinrich Wolfflin, whose Principles of Art History narrates its development as a move to "painterly" style and "relative clarity." This term was originally derisive, coming from a term for a (*) misshapen pearl. Opera originated in this era. In music and architecture, this style was characterized by a profusion of ornaments. It is often linked to the artistic "populism" of the Counter-Reformation, exemplified by "grand" history paintings. This style was pioneered by Bernini and Caravaggio. For 10 points, give this general term for art of the 17th century.
2.r: Baroque

2.q: A colorful, lightweight, cotton slub fabric woven in this pattern is named for its origins in Chennai. One common name for this pattern originates from a blanket-like garment wrapped around the chest and draped over the left shoulder. A trademarked design for this pattern was originally used for the lining of gabardine trench coats. Madras fabrics feature this pattern. A (*) tan design for this pattern featuring black and white perpendicular stripes with red accents is a signature of Burberry. The Black Watch and royal Stewart designs for this pattern are traditional to Highland clans. For 10 points, name this pattern similar to checks that is often used for flannel shirts and Scottish kilts.
2.r: plaid [or tartan; prompt on Burberry Check or checkers; prompt on madras until read by asking “what pattern on the fabric?”]

2.q: This poem's speaker notes that we trust "that nothing walks with aimless feet" and that "somehow good will be the final goal of ill" before lamenting that he is "an infant crying in the night; and with no language but a cry". Its epilogue describes the wedding of the poet's sister, while its early sections relate its addressee's journey from Venice to the banks of the Severn. A late section of this poem is sometimes excerpted as "Ring Out, Wild Bells". This poem asks "are God and Nature then at strife?", describing the latter as (*) "red in tooth and claw". Its 84th canto relates a "truth that came with bier and pall", namely that "'tis better to have loved and lost, than never to have loved at all". For 10 points, identify this poem written as a requiem for the late Arthur Henry Hallam, a work of Alfred, Lord Tennyson.
2.r: “In Memoriam A.H.H.”
2.c: 2013 Minnesota Undergraduate Tournament (MUT) Pkt HPacket 8 Proofread Q20

2.q: This person was told "There is nothing new except what has been forgotten" by a designer posthumously nicknamed "Rose." Either Thomas More or this person lends their name to canities subita, a dubious syndrome of stress turning hair white overnight. A scandalously intimate portrait of this person holding a rose and wearing a muslin dress was quickly repainted into a similar pose of her wearing blue in a garden. A naval victory prompted this woman to wear a model (*) ship in her hair, which was managed by her coiffeur Leonard Autie. This woman, the most famous subject of portraits by Elisabeth Vigee Le Brun, popularized the pouf hairstyle in France. For 10 points, name this queen whose influence on fashion only increased after she was driven out of the Palace of Versailles.
2.r: Marie Antoinette [or Maria Antonia Josefa Johanna or Marie Antoinette Josèphe Jeanne]

2.q: Maria Martinez is best known for her work in this medium, in which she pioneered its "Black on Black" style. Camille Le Tallec made works in this medium in the Vincennes and Sevres styles. The Moche culture of Peru produced detailed types of these works in the shapes of human heads. Shoji Hamada work mostly in this medium, and the Jomon period of Japanese history was renowned for its works of art in this medium. The Etruscans produced types of this artwork called Bucchero. The (*) Andokides Painter may have invented the red-figure style used on Greek examples of these works called amphoras. For 10 points, name these vessels that can be created by using clay with a wheel and firing it in a kiln.
2.r: pottery [accept ceramics; accept vases or vase painting; accept porcelain]
2.c: 2018 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt G. Packet 7 Q11

2.q: This fashion house forced out its second director after he was conscripted shortly after a poorly received 1960 beatnik-inspired show. The feature item from this house's 1955 line was a flared jacked over a dress with a full, pleated skirt, a design that introduced its designer's "A-Line" style that was popularized with the 1958 "Trapeze Line." (*) Coco Chanel quipped "Only a man who never was intimate with a woman could design something that uncomfortable" about one of this house's shows. This house, which is credited with inventing the modern pencil skirt, is often credited with revitalizing post-World War II French fashion with its 1947 New Look show. This house's second director, who used his own label to popularize female tuxedos, was Yves Saint Laurent. For 10 points, name this fashion house named for its founder, Christian.
2.r: Christian Dior SE

2.q: Two mittens that say "Moi" and "Toi" sit next to one of these objects in the Louise Bourgeois [boor-ZHWA] installation piece Child and Parents. Mad for Real members Yuan Chai and Jun Xi jumped on one of these objects designed by Tracey Emin. For the performance art piece Carry That Weight, Columbia University student Emma Sulkowicz (*) carried around one of these objects in protest of sexual assault. For 10 points, identify these objects used in performance art that consist of pillows and sheets.
2.r: <u>bed</u>s [or <u>mattress</u>es]

2.q: An essay by Clifford Geertz opens by stating that this discipline is "notoriously hard to talk about" and is titled for "[this discipline] as a Cultural System." It's not culture, but an important work in the anthropology of this discipline is a Claude Levi-Strauss book titled for the primitive form of this discipline. Another work about this discipline discusses how the products of this discipline have lost their (*) "aura" due to mass mechanization. For 10 points, name this discipline about which Walter Benjamin wrote "in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction" that includes production of works like sculptures and paintings.
2.r: art [accept Art as a Cultural System; accept Primitive Art; accept The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction]
2.c: 2018 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt B. Packet 2 Q19

2.q: Banksy paired the famous image of Vietnam's "Napalm Girl" with Mickey Mouse and this marketing character. Arab Christians rioted in protest of a sculpture of this advertising mascot crucified in 2019 at a museum in Haifa, Israel. Charity housing for families of hospitalized children (*) under 21 is provided under this character's name by the restaurant he represents. Friends of this figure include Grimace, Mayor McCheese, and the Hamburglar. For 10 points, who is this mascot of a fast food franchise known for its golden arches?
2.r: <u>Ronald McDonald</u> [need full name]

2.q: The composer Samuel Coleridge-Taylor used one of these works for his overture to Hiawatha's Wedding Feast. These songs inspired the third movement of a "Tone Journey" by Ferde Grofe ["FER-dee gro-FAY"] whose last section depicts Fat Tuesday. These works play the part of a chorale in a piece written in response to Kristallnacht, Michael Tippett's oratorio A Child of Our Time. Michael Steinberg claims that one of these songs inspired a flute solo in the first movement of a symphony in E minor, whose (*) Largo second movement was adapted into one of these works by William Arms Fisher. These songs inspired Grofe's Mississippi Suite and Antonin Dvorak's Symphony No. 9 "From the New World." For 10 points, "Go Down Moses" and "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot?" are examples of what kind of religious songs created by African-Americans?
2.r: spirituals [or Negro melodies; prompt on folk songs, prompt on hymns, prompt on answers like gospel songs or blues songs]

2.q: Philippe Cassegrain created an origami-inspired style of these objects named Le Pliage. Takashi Murakami first found fame in the West for drawing "Monogramouflage" designs on these objects. They aren't food or jewellery, but a Season 3 episode of Sex and the City popularised the "Baguette" type of these objects. The intrecciato technique of manufacturing these objects is the trademark of (*) Bottega Veneta. Designs of these objects that placed labels on their exterior were a signature of Kate Spade. Following a chance meeting on a flight, Hermes ("er-MEZ") began selling a notoriously expensive type of these objects named after Jane Birkin, who complained about their lack of pockets or handles. For 10 points, Louis Vuitton sell monogrammed designs of what fashion accessories, used to carry personal items?
2.r: handbags [or purses, accept tote bags, accept clutches, accept Longchamp bag, accept Birkin bag until read]

2.q: One character in this work has to have a book removed from his rectum after he breaks into a military camp. One minor character in this work describes how he didn't visit his sister on her deathbed because he was in line for a new iPhone at the Apple Store. One character in this work repeatedly interrupts other characters to declare that he has (*) maggots in his scrotum. A group of characters in this work sing a song about the phrase "Hasa Diga Eebowai," which they claim means "Fuck You God" but doesn't actually mean anything in any real language. One character in this musical sings a song about an "All-American Prophet." For 10 points, name this musical set in Uganda featuring missionaries from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints.
2.r: The Book of Mormon

2.q: This designer routinely sold ready-to-wear versions of his fisherman's shirt, safari jacket, and beatnik-inspired designs at his Rive Gauche boutique. For his debut collection, this designer reimagined [emphasize] another designer's "A-line" skirt design into a full-silhouette "trapeze" concept. This designer prominently featured white, red, blue, and yellow monochromatic blocks in the design of six cocktail dresses he created for his (*) Mondrian Collection. In 1966, this designer unveiled his "Le Smoking" line, a series of tuxedo suits tailored for women. After the death of Christian Dior, this designer was named the head artistic director of his teacher Dior's label at the age of 21. For 10 points, the name of which Algerian-born French fashion designer can be shortened to YSL?
2.r: Yves Saint Laurent [or Yves Henri Donat Mathieu-Saint-Laurent; accept YSL until “YSL” is read]

2.q: An exhibition at Old Bond Street named for these items displays an Alexander McQueen dress that dropped these items as the finale look of his 2007 Sarabande runway show. In 1992, Christy Turlington modeled a black Chanel (sha-NELL) dress with gold chains attached to embellishments shaped like these items. They're not animals, but these items appear in a colorful Gucci pattern designed for Grace Kelly that was inspired by Botticelli's (*) Primavera. In 19th-century England, accessories called tussie-mussies were examples of these items that were given meaning according to a "Victorian language." Crowns made of these items are popular in bohemian style and frequently appear in Frida Kahlo's self-portraits. Boutonnieres and corsages are made of, for 10 points, what items that include camellias and roses?
2.r: flowers [or roses or camellias before mention; prompt on bouquets]

2.q: This is the title of the reggae-infused ballad that was the lead single of K-Pop singer Taeyeon's 2019 album Purpose. This was the name of the directorial debut of Alan Alda. This is the name of the real-life hotel chain that was used to film the HBO series The White Lotus. Manhattan's Seagram Building is home to a restaurant with this name, which has walls adorned with Rothko paintings. A band with this name sang (*) "what a lady, what a night" in a song about a night in 1963. This is the name of a pizza topped with artichokes, basil, mushrooms, and ham. The musical Jersey Boys is about a band of this name. This is the name of a band led by Frankie Valli. For 10 points, what is the English name of pizza quattro Stagioni?
2.r: Four Seasons [accept quattro Stagioni before mentioned]

3.q: A designer from this country known for her trademark pink bob-and-fringe cut created the safety-pin heavy Conceptual Chic collection. Astronomy magazines about Saturn inspired a designer from this country to create an orb pendant. A model from this country applied three layers of false eyelashes to achieve her signature androgynous look. At the 1965 Melbourne Derby Day, a model from this country nicknamed the (*) "Shrimp" arrived late wearing a white minidress sans stockings or gloves. Girl groups like the Ronettes inspired the beehive hairdo of an R&B singer from this country, whose "swinging" and "mod" 60s counterculture fashion was pioneered by the Sex boutique and models like Twiggy. For 10 points, Vivienne Westwood is from what country whose design award is named for the Queen?
3.r: England [accept Great Britain; accept United Kingdom; reject “Scotland,” “Wales,” or “Northern Ireland”] (The designer mentioned in the lead-in is Zandra Rhodes. Vivienne Westwood created the orb pendant, which features in her brand’s logo. The “Shrimp” is Jean Shrimpton. The singer is Amy Winehouse.)

3.q: In the first movement of Charles Ives's Holidays Symphony, this song competes with "The Campbells Are Coming" before the orchestra quietly plays "Pig Town Fling." Samuel Bayard argued that this song's melody is a composite of the Scottish folk tunes "The Black Eagle" and "The Rose Tree." In the 1830s, blackface minstrel performer George Washington Dixon popularized an astoundingly racist song with the same melody, called "Zip Coon." A goat devours the sheet music for this song during a performance in which nursing (*) piglets have their tails pulled and a cow's teeth are turned into a makeshift xylophone by Mickey Mouse as this song plays in "Steamboat Willie." This song, whose lyrics include "went out to milk, and I didn't know how / I milked the goat instead of a cow," is one of the most common mainstays of American ice cream trucks. For 10 points, identify this song traditionally played on fiddles during rural dances, named for a barnyard animal who is also referred to as being "in the hay."
3.r: “Turkey in the Straw”

3.q: An essay about this thing opens "Keep always this dim corner for me," as the author watches its "hour" glide a "proud pavane of Time"; that essay by Aleister Crowley notes that this thing's name means "undelightful." Rehnhjelm and Falander discuss theater and consume this substance in a chapter named after it in The Red Room. A woman in Waiting at Grenelle is featured with her back turned to the viewer as she consumes this thing in a painting by Toulouse-Lautrec. A character in "All the King's Men" calls this substance with (*) rye the best hangover cure, and Oscar Wilde compared it to a sunset. A Picasso portrait of Angel Fernandez de Soto features this thing, and a Picasso sculpture named for it contains a sugar cube sitting on a spoon. For 10 points, name this titular "green fairy" pictured alongside a miserable woman in a painting by Degas.
3.r: absinthe [prompt on answers like the green goddess or the green fairy (until mentioned)]

3.q: This artist wrote "tell us when you first noticed the sky" in a collection with abstract dot-drawings called Acorn. "Anti-films" by this artist include slow-motion shots of burning matches. Viewers climb a ladder and use a magnifying glass to see a tiny "yes" on the ceiling in a piece by this artist. Performers enter a black bag where they can see but not be seen in a piece by this artist, which shares its name with their concept of "bagism." Instructions like "keep coughing a year" are collected in this artist's (*) Grapefruit. This artist invited the audience to remove pieces of her clothing in one performance. This artist formed a "plastic band" with her husband, who posed nude with her in an Annie Leibovitz photo. For 10 points, name this Fluxus artist of Cut Piece who composed "Revolution 9" with John Lennon.
3.r: Yoko Ono [or Ono Yōko; accept Plastic Ono Band]

3.q: This music critic praised one opera for articulating a vision of love as the "deadly hatred of the sexes." This critic compared a different composer's orchestration to a "sirocco" wind and wrote of that composer, is he "a human being at all? Is he not rather a disease?" This critic wrote "Yesterday I heard...Bizet's masterpiece, for the twentieth time" to begin a book of essays which label a different composer as a "Danger" and an "Apostle of Chastity." This critic's own compositions include a (*) Hymn to Friendship for piano and the choral piece Hymn to Life, which he once conducted in Bayreuth ("BYE-royt") for his friend Cosima. This critic claimed that themes of Parsifal ("PART-zee-vall"), particularly its Christianity, signalled its composer's "hatred of life" in a book he wrote "contra" his erstwhile friend Richard Wagner. For 10 points, what philosopher argued that opera exemplified "Socratic culture" in his book about Apollonian and Dionysian influences, titled The Birth of Tragedy?
3.r: Friedrich Nietzsche

3.q: Some scholars suggest that the figure directly behind and to the right of Joseph in Michelangelo's Doni Tondo was based off this figure. In 1532, Giovanni Montorsoli attempted to recreate the missing right arm of this figure, but it was later replaced after Ludwig Pollak discovered the real one in 1905. Similarities that a sculpture depicting this figure has with the Great Altar of Zeus leads scholars to conclude that that sculpture was created in Pergamon and not in Rhodes. The face of Homer in Raphael's (*) Parnassus is copied from the face of this figure. Pope Clement VII commissioned Baccio Bandinelli to create several smaller copies of a sculpture depicting this figure, including one sent as a gift to Francis I. This figure's son, Antiphantes, stares in horror as he is being killed in the most famous sculpture which he appears in. For 10 points, name this Trojan priest who appears in an oft-copied Roman sculpture that depicts him being killed by snakes.
3.r: Laocoon [accept Laocoonand His Sons]

3.q: A conductor from this country faced calls to resign from the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra in 2013 after he claimed that orchestras "react better" to male conductors. A different conductor from this country was music director of the London Symphony Orchestra from 2007 to 2017 and often conducts with a toothpick. A composer from this country wrote an opera in which Renata obsessively searches for her love Madiel and is sentenced to be burned at the stake. The composer of (*) The Fiery Angel and Love for Three Oranges was from this country, as was a composer who turned away from opera after he was attacked in the article "Muddle Instead of Music" for formalism and coarseness. For 10 points, name this home country of Sergei Prokofiev and Dmitri Shostakovich.
3.r: Russia [accept Soviet Union or USSR] (Every person in this tossup was alive during either the formation or the fall of the Soviet Union; the conductors in the first two sentences are Vasily Petrenko and Valery Gergiev, respectively.)

3.q: This symphony's first movement was originally intended to end after a melancholy bassoon solo played over dissonant ninetuplets in the strings. James Hepokoski's monograph on this symphony argues that its G major slow movement, which presents variations on a descending theme introduced by flutes, then pizzicato strings, exemplifies its "rotational form." It begins with a timpani roll on low B-flat, followed by a rising theme in the horns, before woodwinds introduce the rising theme [read slowly] "E-flat, F, C." Six loud, isolated tutti chords conclude this symphony, whose most salient theme is introduced by (*) four horns playing the tied half notes [read slowly] "B-flat, up a fifth to E-flat, back down to B-flat." This symphony's composer merged its slow first movement with its second-movement scherzo in a late 1915 revision and centered its finale on a theme inspired by the flight of sixteen swans. For 10 points, name this E-flat major symphony by Jean Sibelius.
3.r: Symphony No. 5 by Jean Sibelius [accept equivalent answers like Sibelius’s Fifth; accept 5 or Fifth after “Sibelius”; prompt on Symphony No. 5 in E-flat or Fifth Symphony]

3.q: Note to players: This tossup is looking for a region that encompasses multiple countries. You may give the name of the general region or any of the individual countries. Joe Boyd produced an album for a clarinetist from this transnational region that popularized "wedding music" in the West. The non-binary artist Azis is the most popular performer of this region's chalga music. Marcel Cellier created a vocal ensemble from this region that was inspired by the music of Filip Kutev. A country in this region is the origin of the small taraf ensemble, and was also the home of a musician who created the anthem (*) "Gelem Gelem" as well as nationalistic "turbo-folk." Recitations of epics from this region are accompanied by the stringed gusle ("goos-lay"). The southernmost country in this region is the origin of the stringed bouzouki and the home of the composer of the scores for Blade Runner and Chariots of Fire. For 10 points, klezmer music originated from Ashkenazi Jews living in what Eastern European peninsula?
3.r: Balkan Peninsula [accept Bulgaria, Serbia, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Slovenia, Croatia, or Greece; prompt on Eastern Europe until “Eastern European” is read]
3.c: 2023 Chicago Open Pkt 19 - Tiebreakers and Extras Q9

3.q: An artist from this country critiqued the exploitation of labor in a recent installation that replaced the U.N. flags in Rockefeller Center with jute bags. Photographs by Felicia Abban line the walls of a pavilion called "[this country] Freedom" at the 2019 Venice Biennale. David Adjaye's parents were from this country, where tourists buy small wooden fertility figures with disc-like heads that are called akua'ba. This country is home to an art form whose name in the Ga language can be translated as "proverb boxes" and which takes the form of large, painted (*) wood sculptures of objects like cigarette boxes and airplanes. Funerals in this country often use those vibrant "fantasy coffins." An artist born in this country uses recycled materials such as bottle caps to make shimmering sheets resembling cloth. For 10 points, name this African country home to the artist El Anatsui, whose Akan people make kente cloth.
3.r: Ghana

3.q: Insects appear over fighting knights in these artists' piece "Deatho Knocko." Two men in yellow run into a stream of wine being poured next to floating heads in these artists' "Drunk with God." Red-faced men are connected by their beards and have beards forming key-shapes in these artists' "Beard Pictures." These artists show versions of themselves in red, blue, and green in "Doubles." These artists were criticized for glorifying skinheads in their controversial "Naked Shit Pictures." These artists' "Jack Freak Pictures" often show maps of the (*) East End, or depicts them in Union Jack patterned outfits. In one piece, these Tory artists appeared in their signature suits while singing "Underneath the Arches" for an entire day. For 10 points, name this couple of performance artists, who describe themselves as "living sculpture."
3.r: Gilbert and George [accept Gilbert Prousch and George Passmore]

3.q: An early collection by this fashion designer was lost when the items were left in trash bags outside a club and thrown away. This designer exhibited a dress made of ostrich feathers and microscope slides painted red at a show whose models were enclosed in an asylum-like mirrored box. A Scottish-inspired collection by this designer was exhibited in a glass pyramid and ended with a life-sized projection made using Pepper's Ghost. This designer's friendship with (*) Lady Gaga inspired the latter to wear this designer's armadillo heels while debuting "Bad Romance" at this designer's collection Plato's Atlantis. This designer's hologram of Kate Moss was displayed at the Met's retrospective on him, Savage Beauty. For 10 points, skull scarves and low-cut "bumster" trousers are iconic looks by what rebellious British fashion designer who committed suicide in 2010?
3.r: Alexander McQueen [or Lee Alexander McQueen] (The first three collections are Taxi Driver, Voss, and The Widows of Culloden.)

3.q: Along with hats, Felicien Trewey used this art form to mimic celebrities as part of his internationally touring performance. A form of animation influenced by papercutting and this art form was pioneered by Lotte Reiniger, who used it in her Adventures of Prince Achmed. Clown-servant characters appearing in one type of this art form include the androgynous Semar. Popular in coffeehouses, Karagoz and Hacivat ("hah-jee-VAHT") are stock characters in a Turkish type of this art form. At the beginning and end of performances of this art form, a triangular gunungan is manipulated by a (*) dalang. Wayang is an Indonesian variant of this art form that employs puppets. Performers can contort their hands to create examples of these phenomena on screens. For 10 points, those plays use what dark regions created by objects blocking light?
3.r: shadows [accept shadowgraphy; accept shadow paintings; accept shadow play or shadow puppetry; accept silhouettes; prompt on puppets by asking “what phenomena do the puppets create?”; reject “outlines”] (Reiniger started papercutting and staging home shadow theater productions of Shakespeare early in life.)

3.q: One music video recorded by an artist singing in this language contains poorly green screened shots of him dancing in locales such as Antarctica and Easter Island. It's not French, but one artist who records in this language duetted with Ziggy Marley on his song "Madanite." The rapper El General and the singer of "We Will Stay Here" are prominent protest musicians in this language. This language is used by a trio of sisters, whose most famous song is an adaptation of a folk song, whose title translates as "love of my heart." That trio is (*) A-WA. Cheb Mami sings in the rai genre in this language, and a concert by one singer in this language, Umm Kholtoum, caused Muammar Qaddafi to postpone a military coup. For 10 points, name this language spoken in countries such as Algeria and Syria.
3.r: Arabic [or Levantine Arabic; or Mashriqi; or Shaami; or Yemeni; or Egyptian Arabic; or Maghribi Arabic]
3.c: 2017 WAO II Pkt 13 Michigan B + Brownstein Q8

3.q: In 1988, this designer created the interior for a car featuring seats upholstered in black and white stripes with red trimming. This designer played with new materials because they wanted "relaxed clothes suited to the actions of normal life," from which their signature wet-look waterproofs were born. A tagline describing "The best-dressed doll in the world", was given to a doll designed by this person named (*) Daisy.This designer was the first to make clothes from PVC and created men's cardigans long enough to be worn as dresses. When discussing an item of clothing pioneered by this designer, she said "they allowed women to run for a bus ... and were much, much sexier". For 10 points, name this British fashion designer associated with the swinging sixties, commonly credited with pioneering the hotpants and mini-skirt.
3.r: Mary Quant [or Dame Barbara Mary Quant]

3.q: Note: specific English term required. Australia-based artist Nusra Qureshi is known for reviving this art form in works like The Ideal Floral Background. This art form has been reimagined in works like Disruption as Rapture and 2009's Provenance, The Invisible Hand by Shahzia Sikander. In a trope sometimes imitated by Renaissance painters, works in this art form often depicted angels with multicolored wings. Reza Abbasi is often called the last great master of this art form, works of which were collected along with (*) calligraphy in albums called Muraqqa. This art form is named for a lead-based red pigment. Abd al-Samad introduced this art form to the Mughal Empire from Persia, where it itself derived from Chinese models, and it was used to paint portraits of patrons like Queen Elizabeth I by Nicholas Hilliard. For 10 points, give this term for the paintings in an illuminated manuscript, which are often small.
3.r: miniatures [accept more specific answers like Persian miniatures; prompt on manuscripts or illuminations before mention; prompt on painting by asking “In what format?”] (The pigment is “minius.”)

3.q: For one song, this person convinced saxophonist Tom Scott to play the Lyricon wind synthesizer while the main artist recorded overdubs through a cardboard tube. This frequent collaborator of Bruce Swedien released a song named for the Japanese title of the explicit film In the Realm of the Senses, convinced a more famous artist to cover Yellow Magic Orchestra's "Behind the Mask," and inspired the stage name of Studio Ghibli's composer. Miles Davis's final album was conducted by this person at the Montreux Jazz Festival. This student of (*) Nadia Boulanger composed the scores for 1985's The Color Purple, In the Heat of the Night, and The Wiz. Beyonce and Georg Solti ("SHOL-tee") are the only people with more Grammys than this producer, who won for his work on "P.Y.T. (Pretty Young Thing)" and "We Are the World." For 10 points, name this producer of Michael Jackson's albums Bad and Thriller.
3.r: Quincy Jones [or Quincy Delight Jones, Jr.] (The song in the lead-in is “Smooth Criminal.” The song named for In the Realm of the Senses is “Ai No Corrida.” Studio Ghibli composer Joe Hisaishi took his stage name from a translation of the name Quincy Jones.)

3.q: This is the suffix of the third track's title on a live album recorded at Boston's Storyville nightclub in 1953. The title of a song composed by Little Benny Harris whose melody begins [read slowly] "low D, G, A, B, C, D [pause], B, C, D [pause], B, low G" ends with this suffix. The title of a composition originally named "Thriving on a Riff" ends in this suffix. In the title of song recorded by Dial Records in 1947, these five letters are appended to the word (*) "Craze." Charlie Parker reworked "How High the Moon" into a song whose title ends with this suffix; that title references Parker's nickname, "Bird." For 10 points, give this five-letter suffix that appears after "Anthrop-" and "Ornith-" in the titles of Charlie Parker songs.
3.r: -ology [accept answers that spell it out; accept “Ornithology,” “Anthropology,” and “Crazeology”]

3.q: "Ideal" and "Presentational" theories of these objects were attacked in a 1968 book that analyzes them using the type-token distinction and describes them as Wittgensteinian "forms of life." A debate with Alain Pessin has been added to a 1983 book about the networks of people who create these things, which was written by Howard S. Becker. Philippe Aries's Centuries of Childhood has been criticized for its reliance on these things as primary sources. Some differences between seemingly identical objects of this kind are detailed at the beginning of The (*) Transfiguration of the Commonplace by Arthur Danto. The "thingly" character of these objects is examined in a 1936 essay collected in the book Poetry, Language, Thought. These things were interpreted as static and spatial, as opposed to the temporality of poetry, in Gotthold Ephraim Lessing's Laocoon. Martin Heidegger explored the "origin" of-for 10 points-what things whose "aura" Walter Benjamin claimed is lost in "the Age of Mechanical Reproduction"?
3.r: works of art [accept either; accept more specific answers like paintings; accept artworlds] (The first book is Richard Wollheim’s Art and Its Objects.)

3.q: This figure names a movement whose first theme ends with three separated unison chords followed by a flute solo on the notes long A, B-flat, D-flat, F, E, B, low F-sharp. Earlier in that movement named for this figure, a driving wind beat accompanies the strings playing a theme beginning long C-sharp, short E, G, long F-sharp, short high B, long A-sharp. The directions "as if in parody" and "sedately, with humor" appear in a Mahler Lied about this figure. A set of variations sometimes named for this non-composer figure opens with oboes and bassoons stating a theme beginning dotted-eighth note D, sixteenth note E-flat, two eighth note D's, quarter notes walking down from (*) E-flat to B-flat. That theme, which despite its common attribution is likely either a pilgrim folk tune or by Ignaz Pleyel, was taken from a second movement named for this figure in a B-flat major divertimento. For 10 points, name this religious figure whose "chorale" inspired Brahms's Variations on a Theme by Haydn and who names a movement of Mathis der Maler depicting their "temptation."
3.r: Saint Anthony of Padua [or Saint Anthony of Lisbon; accept Antony or Antonius; accept Fernando Martins de Bulhões or Fernando]

3.q: One piece with this text uses a tape recording of a "wind harp" to evoke the Ison of Byzantine music, calls for an amplified prepared piano with metal screws, and was written by Arvo Part. This text is sung by the choir in the second part of Havergal Brian's "Gothic" Symphony. This text is sometimes paired with the Jubilate in the Anglican tradition, as in Herbert Howells's Collegium Regale, and William Walton wrote a setting of this text for the coronation of Elizabeth II. A Marche en rondeau serves as the prelude to a piece of this type in D major by (*) Marc-Antoine Charpentier. A five-movement one in C major was written by Anton Bruckner, who considered using it as the finale of his 9th symphony. Handel composed a piece of this type to commemorate the English victory at the Battle of Dettingen. During a performance of his own piece of this type, Jean-Baptiste Lully fatally injured himself with his conducting staff. For 10 points, identify this Christian hymn whose opening proclaims "We praise thee, O God."

About halfway through this piece, the left hand holds a chord on A-sharp and C-sharp while the right hand ascends the keyboard in rapid chromatic trills. A biography by a non-DJ Alan Walker compares the passage leading to this piece's conclusion -- which begins with the hands simultaneously playing two octaves of descending and ascending chromatic chords -- to its composer's Technical Exercises. This piece revises and transposes the composer's earlier A minor Grande Fantaisie de Bravoure based on the same rondo theme, which was also arranged for violin and piano by (*) Fritz Kreisler. It is the third of a set of six studies written for Clara Schumann and revised in 1851. This piece takes its main theme from an Italian composer's Violin Concerto No. 2 in B minor and evokes its namesake object by repeatedly playing the highest D-flat on the piano. For 10 points, what piece from Liszt's Grandes Etudes de Paganini is named for the Italian word for "little bell?"
3.r: “La campanella” [or Étude No. 3 in G♯ minor from the Grandes Études de Paganini]

3.q: A biography by Aaron Firsch is titled for a "dark" one of these people. An album by Gil Shaham is titled for one of these people "of the opera." Walter Wilson Cobbett compared the third movement of "Death and the Maiden" to a dance of one of these people. Two of these people title a children's opera by Peter Maxwell Davies based on a Mackay Brown short story. A parody musical replaces one of these characters with the Lovecraftian Shoggoth. An operatic character with this title lays claim to the land between the (*) farms of Marti and Manz, and later plays music over the deuteragonists' suicide; that opera is Delius's A Village Romeo and Juliet. For 10 points, a Jerry Bock musical is titled for what sort of instrumentalist "on the roof?"
3.r: fiddler [accept Dark Fiddler or demon fiddler; prompt on descriptions like violinist; prompt on demon]

3.q: A band named in homage of this group released the album We Are the Halluci Nation and combines hip hop with traditional First Nations music. This group asked questions like "What is sex when you have three people?" and "What are laws if they ain't fair and equal?", and they sampled Bennie and the Jets for their song Solid Wall of Sound. Another song by this group behind the song What? pointedly tells minorities that "all you bad folks, you must go." This group sampled Jimmy McGriff's Green Dolphin Street for their song Jazz (We Got), and on the song We Can Get Down, the title program of one album by this group states this band's members are (*) "Phife Dawg, Ali Shaheed Muhammad, Q-Tip, and Jarobi." After a 20 year hiatus, this group behind the songs We the People... and Electric Relaxation released the album We Got It from Here ... Thank You 4 Your Service. For 10 points, name this jazz rap group behind the albums Midnight Marauders and The Low End Theory.
3.r: A Tribe Called Quest [accept ATCQ; the rap group in the lead in is “A Tribe Called Red”]

3.q: An entity that describes itself as "the Orphan Ship of State" breaks news about a member of this family to the title character of a Jeanine Tesori musical set in Louisiana. Beth, Charley, and Franklin perform a number that satirizes the "rows and rows and rows" of members of this family in the musical Merrily We Roll Along. An institution named for a member of this family hosts the Broadway Center Stage performance series. An ascending F-major triad brass motif represents the title of a musical associated with this (*) real-life family, whose lead roles were originated by Richard Burton and Julie Andrews. A member of this family associated that Lerner and Loewe ("low") musical with her husband in a 1963 interview with Life magazine. For 10 points, a member of what family is associated with the musical Camelot and names a performing arts center in Washington, DC?
3.r: Kennedy [accept the Kennedys; accept Jacqueline Onassis Kennedy or John Fitzgerald Kennedy] (The first line refers to the musical Caroline, or Change.)
3.c: 2023 Chicago Open Pkt 07 - Kasiński et al, Marvin et al Q14

3.q: An artist from this country filmed a nine-shot, 132-minute film in which her family prepares then eats a meal, Oxhide II. A 1989 Avant-Garde exhibition in this country was shut down after an artist shot her own piece, Dialogue. Two artists from this country created a robot arm that danced while oil leaked from it, eventually becoming sidetracked by trying to plug its holes. 1,001 people from this country were invited to 2007 Documenta with outfits designed by an artist from here who helped design a (*) stadium for Herzog & de Meuron. An artist from this country created a series of photos of his outstretched arm giving the middle finger to world monuments. 3.q: The workshop of Georg Siegmund Stobwasser was renowned for making snuff boxes from this material. Many Latin American festivals feature people whipping children and young women with pig bladders while wearing costumes made of this material. After Russian icon painting fell out of fashion, unemployed artists turned to lacquering boxes and panels made of this material. Because French troops ransacked the Vatican, Pope Pius VII had to be crowned with a tiara made of this material during his 1800 coronation. Egyptian funerary (*) masks from the First Intermediate Period onwards used a material similar to this one, known as cartonnage. Three-dimensional Korean hanji art uses a material very similar to this one. This medium grew in popularity in 18th century England and France as a cheaper replacement for wood and plaster, though it was itself largely supplanted by plastic. Cloth, pottery, and this material are commonly used to create pinatas. For 10 points, name this composite material made by binding sheets of paper with glue, whose name means "chewed paper" in French.
3.r: papier-mache [prompt on paper before it is read]

3.q: After leaving Fletcher Henderson's band, Don Redman became director of a group named after this substance. That group was led by William McKinney. This is the first word in the title of a Duke Ellington composition whose melody begins with the figure [read slowly] "quarter rest, quarter note C, eighth notes low G, B-flat," quarter note D, dotted quarter note C, eighth note C. In 1934, Adelaide Hall and a young Lena Horne starred in a "parade" at a (*) venue named for this substance, which was segregated, unlike the rival Savoy Ballroom. 3.q: The Charles Hosmer Morse Museum houses the most comprehensive collection of this artist's works. Benjamin Harrison's widow Mary Dimmick commissioned a work by this artist that depicts Archangel Michael in chainmail. Works etched with this artist's initials were usually made by a team of assistants who had learned under Arthur Nash. Edward Colonna created silver-gilt mounts for works attributed to this artist. This artist's namesake (*) "Girls" were employed under the supervision of Clara Driscoll. Knockoffs of this artist's signature products were popularized by restaurants such as T. G. I. Fridays. This artist's signature Wisteria Tree was often featured on products made of his trademarked "favrile" material. For 10 points, name this artist whose company made eponymous glass lamps.

3.c: 2023 Chicago Open Pkt 11 - Ray et al Q16

3.q: Georges Vantongerloo used this material to create his abstract sculpture Construction of Volume Relations. Most of Louise Nevelson's assemblages, such as Sky Cathedral, consist of found objects made from this material. In Germany, this was the primary medium of artists like Michael Pacher and Veit Stoss. The Church of St. James in Rothenburg displays an altar made from this substance, which contains a relic of the blood of Jesus. This material was used to create The Holy Blood Altar, the masterpiece of Tilman (*) Riemenschneider, as well as many smaller decorative works by Grinling Gibbons. A print created from an artwork made of this material depicts a man holding a balance and an emaciated man riding an emaciated horse. 3.r: wood [or clear equivalents]
3.c: 2015 Chicago Open Pkt 04 - Sizzling Stakhanovite Cycle of Memetics Q14

3.q: Some of these animals are tied to the genitals of a diva played by Matthew Barney in a scene from Cremaster 5. Actors tossed around fake dead examples of these animals at Cannes to promote 24 Hour Party People, in which Ryder and Paul claim to have killed 3,000 of these animals. 3.c: 2023 On Cinema at the Buzzer Pkt 05 Q14

3.q: In Indian art, tribhanga is a version of this technique. Bruce Nauman walked along the perimeter of a square in a 1968 video series where he attempted to emulate this artistic technique in reality titled Walk with [this technique]. In Personal Styles in Greek Sculpture, Adolph H. Borbein associates this technique with a combination of standbein and spielbein. The use of this technique saw a shift away from creating kouroi. The serpentine shape of the (*) "S-curve" derives from a more extreme version of this technique. Polykleitos utilized what he referred to as his "Canon of Proportions" to create one of the earliest examples of this technique in his Doryphoros. The central figure turns his head to the right in Michelangelo's David, creating a line that accentuates an example of this technique. For 10 points, name this artistic technique whereby a figure enters a natural pose by placing all their weight placed on one leg with their arms behind them.
3.r: contrapposto

3.q: A song by this band is built off the melodic figure "E [pause], E, F-sharp, D-sharp [pause]," which is repeated several times before switching to a "C-natural [pause], C, D, B" figure. 3.q: A player of this instrument collaborated with Duke Ellington and Charles Mingus on the tracks "Very Special" and "Fleurette Africaine" for the album Money Jungle. 3.q: The French dentist Laurent Mourguet ("lo-RON moor-GAY") created one of these objects that has since become a symbol of the city of Lyon and its silk workers, the canuts ("kah-NOO"). 3.q: A technique named for this substance was used to make a blue, green, and white sculpture of the Nativity in the Washington National Gallery. 3.q: In 2010, one of these instruments became the most expensive musical instrument ever sold.
